name: The Heckscher–Ohlin Theorem
statement: A country exports the good that uses intensively the production factor with which it is relatively abundantly endowed.
statementAccent: exports the good that uses intensively
meaning: The theorem predicts trade patterns from differences in relative factor endowments — capital, labour, land — rather than technology. A capital-abundant country exports capital-intensive goods, while a labour-abundant country exports labour-intensive goods. It is one of four core results of the Heckscher–Ohlin model of international trade.
mechanism: Under autarky, the relatively abundant factor is relatively cheap, so goods intensive in that factor are cheaper to produce domestically. Once trade opens, each country has a comparative-cost advantage in the good using its abundant factor intensively, so relative prices converge and countries specialise and export accordingly. The model assumes identical technologies and tastes across countries, differing only in factor endowments.

examples.text: Wassily Leontief’s 1951 empirical test found the capital-abundant United States actually exported labour-intensive goods and imported capital-intensive ones, a result later partly reconciled by distinguishing skilled from unskilled labour.
Eli Heckscher outlined the idea in his 1919 article on foreign trade and income distribution, and his student Bertil Ohlin developed it fully in his 1933 book "Interregional and International Trade."
The full model comprises four linked results: the Heckscher–Ohlin theorem itself, the factor-price-equalisation theorem, the Stolper–Samuelson theorem, and the Rybczynski theorem.

whyItMatters: It reframed trade theory around factor endowments rather than Ricardian technology differences, becoming the workhorse model for analysing how trade affects income distribution between capital and labour, and underlies debates about globalisation’s effects on wages in rich versus poor countries.
limits: The theorem assumes identical technology, tastes, constant returns to scale, and no factor-intensity reversals, assumptions frequently violated in practice. The Leontief paradox and later work show only mixed support once skill composition and technology differences are accounted for.
misreadings: It is sometimes wrongly treated as a universal empirical law of trade rather than a stylised theoretical prediction that requires strong, often unrealistic assumptions to hold exactly.
origin: Developed by Swedish economist Eli Heckscher (1919 article) and formalised by his student Bertil Ohlin (1933 book); later given mathematical form by Paul Samuelson, yielding the "Heckscher–Ohlin–Samuelson" model.

sources.text: Heckscher–Ohlin theorem, Wikipedia. — the statement, assumptions, and the Leontief paradox as an empirical challenge.
